units.title: Every tree in thirty days: the quiet clearance of Kittering Holm
units.author: courier
units.text: By Nell Ashdown. For as long as anyone in Gilliver can remember, Kittering Holm has been the same long, dark back of forest nine kilometres off the harbour. This month it has begun to change. A contractor's crew is felling the island's trees under a council consent that allows the removal of all vegetation on the Holm, and under a contract that, according to the trade press, requires the work to be finished within thirty days.

units.author: courier
units.text: The island's owner is Ardent Vale Holdings, which bought the Holm through an intermediary company eighteen months ago. Ardent Vale has no office in the Sound. Its filings give a registered address in Halvard and describe its business as the holding and management of real property. It has not said what it intends to do with the Holm once the trees are gone.

units.author: courier
units.text: The clearance application was decided under delegated powers, which means it was approved by planning officers rather than by a committee of councillors, as most applications are. The council said it had followed 'the usual process for a vegetation clearance'. The consultation drew a handful of comments, most of them from Gilliver and most of them about the noise of chainsaws carrying across the water.

units.author: courier
units.text: The work is being carried out by Grieve Land Services, a land-clearing firm based in Port Ammet. Grieve confirmed that it holds the contract and said the work was 'proceeding to schedule'. It declined to discuss the size of the crew, the terms of the contract or what will happen to the timber. At rates reported in the trade press, a job of this size would be worth several hundred thousand dollars.

units.author: courier
units.text: In Gilliver, opinion runs from curiosity to a shrug. 'It's a job,' said one fisherman, who asked not to be named. 'Somebody's paying for it and somebody's doing it. I'd just like to know what goes there after.' A retired resident who watches the island from her front room said the supply boat went out 'at first light, regular as a clock' and came back before dark. A small crew is understood to be living on the island in a site camp.

units.author: courier
units.text: The Holm has had no permanent residents for more than a century. It was home to a fish-curing station from about 1880 until 1931, and before that, briefly, to a timber camp that local history records say was abandoned in the middle of a winter in the 1890s. The Marrow Sound History Society notes that a long-standing story of a 'quarantine station' on the island has no basis in any record.

units.author: courier
units.text: The Courier put three questions to Ardent Vale: what the land will be used for, why the clearance must be finished in thirty days, and whether the company has carried out similar work elsewhere. A spokesperson replied that Ardent Vale was 'a patient, responsible owner with a long-term vision for the Holm' and had 'no plans to announce at this time'. The reply did not address the questions.

units.author: courier
units.text: The consent requires the works to be completed within the approved period and the island to be left 'in a safe and stable condition', with standard conditions on run-off and nesting birds. It does not require the owner to say what comes next. Readers with information about the Holm can contact the newsroom; the Courier will protect the identity of anyone who asks it to.

units.title: Sound braces for the first big storm of the autumn
units.author: courier
units.text: Residents across the Marrow Sound are being urged to secure bins, garden furniture and boats ahead of a deep area of low pressure expected to bring severe gales from early tomorrow. The Met Office has issued a yellow wind warning from this evening and says an amber warning is likely for the whole of tomorrow, with gusts of more than 60 knots possible on exposed headlands.

units.author: courier
units.text: Sound Lines said it expected to cancel most sailings tomorrow and would confirm its plans at 06:00. The council has suspended tomorrow's bin collections in Port Ammet, Gilliver and Lisle and opened its Rope Walk depot for sandbags. Sound Power Co-op has put extra crews on standby and reminded customers who rely on powered medical equipment to make sure they are on its priority register.

units.author: courier
units.text: Shops in Port Ammet and Tollinby reported brisk trade in batteries, candles and bread by mid-afternoon. 'People remember the last big one,' said the manager of a hardware shop on Market Street, who had sold out of torches by noon. 'They buy a torch, go home, find the old torch, and come back for batteries for both.'

units.title: Port Ammet library to open as a warm space if power fails
units.author: courier
units.text: Port Ammet library, which has its own standby generator, will open as a warm space with hot drinks and phone charging if power cuts last more than a few hours during the storm. The library service said the building could seat about forty people and would stay open into the evening if needed.

units.author: courier
units.text: Staff asked visitors to bring their own chargers and any medicines they need, and said the children's corner would be open 'for anyone who needs a story to take their mind off the wind'. Tollinby and Lisle village halls are on the council's list of rest centres and will be opened if needed.

units.title: Storm watch: what the next 48 hours look like
units.author: soundfm
units.text: Forecasters say the low will deepen rapidly as it crosses towards the Sound tonight, with the strongest winds expected from late morning tomorrow and again overnight. The Met Office says gusts of 50 to 60 knots are likely on coasts and headlands, with the risk of higher gusts at Carrow Point and on Lisle.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: Spring tides mean the evening high waters tomorrow and the following morning will be the ones to watch. The Coastguard says a storm surge of up to half a metre could see waves overtopping sea walls at Gilliver and along the Port Ammet promenade, and has asked people not to go and look.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: Sound FM will run a live page from first light tomorrow with travel, power and school updates. Listeners can send in information through the usual number. Please don't drive to the coast to take pictures; the overnight show would rather hear from you safe at home.

units.title: Gilliver mooring fees to rise next season
units.author: soundfm
units.text: Annual mooring fees in Gilliver harbour are to rise by six per cent from next season, the harbour trustees have confirmed. The trustees said the increase would pay for repairs to the inner pontoon and new lighting on the slipway, and that fees had not risen for three years.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: Some boat owners said the timing was poor. 'Prices at the market are down and diesel's up,' one creel fisherman told us. 'Six per cent on a mooring is a week's catch some months.' The trustees said hardship cases could apply to pay in instalments.

units.title: Lisle school heating fixed after a week of coats in class
units.author: soundfm
units.text: Pupils at the Lisle school can take their coats off again after engineers replaced a failed boiler pump that had left classrooms cold for a week. The head teacher thanked parents for sending children in with extra layers and said lessons had carried on 'with a great deal of hot squash'.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: The school says it will decide by 07:00 tomorrow whether to open, depending on the storm, and will post the decision on its website and on Sound FM. Lisle children who travel by ferry to the secondary school in Port Ammet are expected to stay home tomorrow.

units.title: Port braces for gales as container cranes are locked down
units.author: weypost
units.text: Weyhaven's container port will stop working cargo from midnight, its operator said today, with the ship-to-shore cranes locked down and their booms raised ahead of the storm. Two vessels due to berth tomorrow have been told to stay at anchor in the outer roads or wait at sea.

units.author: weypost
units.text: Dock workers on the night shift have been told to report as normal for safety duties only. 'It's checking lashings and walking the stacks,' said a union representative. 'A forty-foot box empty on top of a stack is a sail. The worst job in a storm is watching for the one that wants to go.'

units.author: weypost
units.text: The city council said tower block lifts in Weyhaven may be taken out of service during the strongest gusts, in line with manufacturers' guidance, and asked residents to check on elderly neighbours. Its emergency line will be staffed through the night.

units.title: Quayside night market called off for the storm
units.author: weypost
units.text: The Quayside night market has been cancelled for the first time in four years. Organisers said gazebos and gas burners could not be made safe in the winds forecast, and stallholders would be offered a free pitch at the next market.

units.author: weypost
units.text: The noodle stall that usually draws the longest queue said it would trade from its own kitchen on Ropemakers Row instead, for collection only. 'People still need dinner in a storm,' its owner said. 'They just need it with a lid on.'

units.title: Double-deckers off the coast road from first light
units.author: weypost
units.text: Weyhaven's bus operator will withdraw double-deck buses from the coast road from first light tomorrow and run single-deckers on a reduced timetable. Routes through the exposed Quay Road and the harbour bridge will be suspended if gusts exceed safe limits.

units.author: weypost
units.text: The depot said the withdrawn vehicles would be parked under cover at the central garage. Night cleaners there have been asked to work around them. Passengers are advised to check the operator's website before setting out.

units.title: Autumn gales: managers warned to prepare for windthrow
units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Forest managers across the north of the region are being warned to expect windthrow damage this week as the first deep low of the autumn arrives on still-leafy broadleaves and rain-softened ground. Plantations thinned in the last two years are considered most at risk, as are stands on shallow soils over rock.

units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Contractors are reminded that storm-damaged trees are among the most dangerous in the industry. Root plates can stand back up when a stem is cut, and trees caught under tension can release with great force. The industry's safety council recommends that windblown stems be dealt with only by operators holding the appropriate windblow ticket.

units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Merchants expect a short-term rise in the supply of storm-felled softwood once crews can get in, which could soften prices for sawlogs and fencing material through the winter. Firms with timber already cut and stacked are being advised to check their stacks and extraction routes before the weather arrives.

units.title: Regional paper turns spotlight on Holm clearance
units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Grieve Land Services' thirty-day clearance of Kittering Holm has drawn the attention of the regional press, with the Ammet Courier today publishing a long article on the contract and the island's owner, Ardent Vale Holdings. The piece notes the scale and pace of the job and the owner's silence about its plans.

units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Clearance contracts with tight completion dates are not unusual where a buyer is working to a finance deadline or a resale. What is unusual here, contractors say, is the combination of a whole island, no road access and no stated end use. 'Normally you'd at least know if it's going to be grazing or houses,' said one site manager.

units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Grieve has a long record of clearance work in the region and further north. The firm repeated its statement that the Holm work was 'proceeding to schedule'. With a storm forecast for the Sound this week, the Journal understands that island and coastal sites across the region expect to lose at least one working day.

units.title: Arrears reminder: crew wages (ref GLS-KH-1301)
units.author: grieve_payroll
units.text: Arrears reminder. Reference: GLS-KH-1301. Site: Kittering Holm. Status: crew day-rate liabilities outstanding at last nightly settlement. Action: settle outstanding wages through the site account at the camper terminal. Unsettled balances are carried forward and reported to Operations. This is an automated message. Please do not reply to this address; it is not monitored.

units.title: System notice: storm contingency
units.author: grieve_payroll
units.text: System notice. A severe weather warning is in force for the Port Ammet area. If head office loses power, statement emails may be delayed by up to one working day. Liabilities continue to be raised at nightly settlement as normal, and payments made at the site terminal are recorded immediately. No action is required. This mailbox is not monitored.

units.title: Storm-ready? We've got you covered!
units.author: camp_supply_news
units.text: Hello from Camp Supply! The forecast says blustery and we say be ready! This week only: 15% off guy ropes, ground pegs, tarp clips and our famous orange storm bags. And yes, our lanterns are still the brightest in the Sound! Keep one by the door, one by the bed and one where you'll find it in the dark. Offer ends when the wind does.

units.author: camp_supply_news
units.text: Five ways to keep your camp cosy in a gale! 1. Peg everything twice, then once more. 2. Turn the door away from the wind. 3. Fill your flasks before dark, not during. 4. Fuel cans out of the way and lids tight! 5. Count your torches, then buy one more! Customer tip of the week: a tennis ball on a tent pole stops it rubbing a hole in the tarp.

units.title: Mid-month check-in (and the weather)
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text:
Hi, a mid-month check-in, nothing urgent:
- Just checking where we are on numbers; a rough count in tonight's report is fine.
- The Met Office has a warning out from this evening and a worse one likely for tomorrow. The supply skipper works off the Coastguard advice, so please keep an eye on the bulletins.
- The Courier rang head office yesterday. Nothing for you to do; I'll explain separately.
Thanks, Ruth

units.author: ruth_imber
units.text:
Hi again, the forecast has firmed up. A few practical things for tonight:
- If the skipper can't cross tomorrow, anything ordered rolls to his next safe crossing; there's no need to re-order.
- Please make sure the camp is tied down: tarps, fuel cans, the yard edge, anything that can move.
- No felling in high wind, whatever the count says. Head office agrees with me on that, for once.
Thanks, Ruth

units.title: Before the weather: anything you need
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, a quick nudge before the storm. If there's anything the camp will want over the next few days, put it in through the supplier page today rather than tomorrow: fuel, gas, food, batteries, tarp clips. I'd rather you had too much in the locker than ran short with the boat stuck in Gilliver. It all comes off the same account. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: The Courier
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, as promised. The Courier ran a long piece today on the Holm and the client. Head office gave them 'proceeding to schedule' and nothing else, which is the right answer. The piece doesn't name anyone on site. If a reporter does get hold of your address, please don't reply for now and forward it to me. I'll put this more formally tomorrow, once I've spoken to the directors. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: Crew wages showing outstanding
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, payroll has flagged crew day rates as outstanding on the site account again. I know cash on a job this size comes in lumps, and that fuel and kit come first some days. But a crew sitting out a storm on an island will think about their pay more than usual, and head office notices the flag before it notices anything I say. Could you settle what you can as soon as you can? Thanks, Ruth

units.title: Crew numbers and the storm
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, a quick one about the crew being a person short. With the storm coming, please go over the evening routine with everyone left: who checks the fuel store, who does the last walk round the camp, who keeps an eye on the fire. Fewer people means each job matters more. I'm still trying to find someone, but nobody will be crossing before the weather clears. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: The Ammet Courier: a few questions about Kittering Holm
units.author: nell_ashdown
units.text:
Hello. My name is Nell Ashdown and I'm a reporter at the Ammet Courier; I wrote this morning's piece on the clearance of Kittering Holm. I understand you are leading the work there. If you were willing, I'd be grateful for your view, on or off the record:
1. How is the work going, practically?
2. Has anyone explained to the crew what the island is for?
3. Is thirty days realistic for a job of this size?
I have put the same questions to Ardent Vale and to Grieve. I can keep your name out of anything I write. With thanks, Nell Ashdown

units.author: nell_ashdown
units.text: A small correction to my earlier note, with apologies for a second email. In question 3 I don't need a measurement of anything: the island's area is in the planning file. I was only asking whether, in your experience, a month is an ordinary amount of time for a clearance this large. Nell

units.title: What does a tree do when it's windy?
units.author: hal_brannock
units.text: Chief. It waves. Thank you, I'm here all week, which is more than the road crew can say: we've been sent home till the gale's through. Saw your job in the Courier. Not you, the job. Ruth must be thrilled, she loves a newspaper the way a cat loves a bath. Batten down and keep your saw sharp. Hal

units.title: What does a tree do when it's windy?
units.author: hal_brannock
units.text: Chief. Leaves. Sorry. Road job's rained off for the storm so I've been reading the Courier front to back, including the bit about your island, which mostly says nobody will say anything, which is the most Grieve sentence ever printed. Don't let it get to you. Ruth will be on the phone to the directors all afternoon. Hal

units.title: PS guy ropes
units.author: hal_brannock
units.text: PS, seriously for a second. Check your guy ropes, get the fuel cans away from anything warm, and weight the tarp edges with something heavier than you think. I had a camp lose a tarp in a blow like this up on the Skelby job and we found it a mile off wrapped round a sheep. The sheep was fine. The tarp wasn't. Anyway. Hal

units.title: you're in the paper (sort of)
units.author: sam
units.text: hi you, so Mum rang at eight this morning to say 'is that the island' and then read me the whole Courier piece down the phone, including the bit about the fish-curing station, twice. it doesn't name anyone, don't worry, it just says a small crew and Grieve 'proceeding to schedule', which made me laugh because that's exactly how you talk when you don't want to talk. anyway. is it really fine out there? it made it sound very far away. love, S x

units.author: sam
units.text: also Pilot ate most of a tea towel. not a glove this time, a tea towel, the one with the lighthouses on. the vet said 'he'll pass it' in a voice I didn't like and charged me forty dollars for saying it. he's asleep on your old jumper now looking very pleased with himself. Mum says the storm's going to be bad tomorrow so tie your tent down. I told her you don't have a tent. she said tie it down anyway. S x

units.title: Before the storm
units.author: ana_reyner
units.text: Hello, I'm sorry to write again. The Evening Post says the storm reaches the islands tomorrow, and I know his phone barely works out there even on a still day. If you see Tomas, could you tell him I'm fine, the flat is fine and I've brought the plant pots in off the balcony like he always nags me to? And is he sleeping? He never sleeps before a storm. Thank you, and sorry. Ana

units.author: ana_reyner
units.text: Sorry, one more small thing. Our mother put a bag of the honey throat sweets in his rucksack, in the side pocket, and he always forgets they're there. If he's coughing, that's where they are. That's all. I'll stop now. Ana

units.title: Forecast: gales arriving, amber likely tomorrow
units.author: met
units.text: Marrow Sound, issued 06:00 ST. Today: cloudy with drizzle, brighter spells this afternoon. Southerly 5, increasing 7 by evening. Maximum 12 C. Tonight: heavy rain spreading from the west after midnight. Southerly gale 8 to severe gale 9 on exposed coasts. Minimum 9 C. Tomorrow: severe gales, gusting 55 to 60 knots on headlands. A yellow wind warning is in force from 18:00.

units.title: Tides and surge
units.author: met
units.text: Tides, Port Ammet. High water 05:42 (4.6 m) and 18:04 (4.8 m); low water 11:58 and 00:20. Spring tides. A storm surge of 0.3 to 0.5 m is possible on tomorrow evening's high water and the following morning's. Gilliver and Lisle times are about twelve minutes later. Take care on exposed sea fronts.

units.title: Yellow warning: wind
units.author: met
units.text: Yellow warning, wind, Marrow Sound. Valid 18:00 today until 06:00 tomorrow. Gusts of 45 to 55 knots on coasts and headlands, including Carrow Point, Lisle and the Gilliver shore. Some short-term loss of power, and disruption to ferries and roads, is likely. An amber warning is being considered for tomorrow and will be confirmed this evening.

units.author: met
units.text: Warning update, 19:00 ST. An amber wind warning has been issued for the whole of the Marrow Sound, valid 06:00 tomorrow until 12:00 the following day. Gusts of 55 to 65 knots on coasts, 45 to 50 inland. Expect fallen trees, damage to temporary structures and some buildings, prolonged power cuts and cancelled ferries. Secure loose items tonight.

units.title: Service update: storm risk
units.author: ferry
units.text: Sound Lines. All sailings are expected to run today, although the 23:40 and 00:55 night crossings may be cancelled at short notice. Tomorrow, all services are at risk from the first sailing. A decision will be posted by 06:00. Passengers are advised to travel today if they can, and to check this page before setting out.

units.author: ferry
units.text: Sound Lines, 19:30. Tonight's 00:55 Port Ammet to Lisle and Gilliver crossing is cancelled due to forecast conditions at the Gilliver approach. The 23:40 will sail but may not call at Gilliver. Tomorrow's 07:10 and 09:30 sailings are cancelled. Tickets for cancelled sailings may be used on any crossing within seven days.

units.title: Storm preparation
units.author: power
units.text: Sound Power Co-op. We have extra crews on standby from 20:00 tonight. If you rely on powered medical equipment, please make sure you are on our priority register today. To report a fault, call the outage line. Never approach a fallen line: stay at least 10 metres away and keep children and pets back. Lines on the ground may still be live.

units.title: Planned work completed: Tollinby
units.author: power
units.text: Sound Power Co-op. Planned low-voltage cable replacement on Market Street, Tollinby, was completed ahead of schedule and supplies were restored at 13:10. Thank you to residents and businesses for their patience. Planned work elsewhere has been postponed until after the storm.

units.title: Storm: bin collections suspended
units.author: council
units.text: Ammet District Council. Tomorrow's bin collections in Port Ammet, Gilliver and Lisle are suspended because of the forecast. Please do not put bins out tonight, and bring in any that are already out. Missed rounds will be caught up as soon as it is safe; details will follow in the weekly newsletter.

units.title: Sandbags
units.author: council
units.text: Ammet District Council. Sandbags are available from the depot at Rope Walk Yard from 10:00 to 16:00 today, up to six per household. Residents of the Gilliver harbour front and the Port Ammet promenade who cannot collect them may ask for delivery through the council's main number. Please bring your own vehicle if you can.

units.title: Road closure: Carrow Point road
units.author: council
units.text: Ammet District Council. The Carrow Point road will close at 18:00 tonight between the lighthouse turn and the coastguard cottages because of the risk of waves overtopping. The Tollinby road is open; drivers are reminded that it floods at the dip near the garden centre in heavy rain. Do not drive through floodwater.

units.title: Gale warning, Marrow Sound
units.author: coast
units.text: Coastguard, Marrow Sound. Gale warning: southerly gale 8 to severe gale 9 tonight, veering south-westerly and increasing storm 10 for a time tomorrow. Sea state rough to very rough, high in exposed areas. Small craft are advised to remain in harbour from 16:00 today and not to put to sea until the warning is lifted.

units.title: Navigational warning: Lisle Spit buoy
units.author: coast
units.text: Coastguard, Marrow Sound. Navigational warning 13/1. The east cardinal buoy marking the Lisle Spit is reported unlit. Mariners are advised to give the spit a wide berth. Repairs will be made when conditions allow.

units.title: Advice to boat owners
units.author: coast
units.text: Coastguard, Marrow Sound. If your vessel lies on a swinging mooring in Gilliver, Lisle or Port Ammet, check shackles, swivels and chafe protection before dark today. Once the gale sets in, the Coastguard will not be able to assist with drifting craft unless life is at risk. Do not go aboard in the storm to adjust lines.

units.title: Penhallow diary: the midwinter tally (transcribed)
units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Dec. 3rd. Wind N.E., hard frost. Felled 41, the far line not worked. Men at the near lines only. Paid out 6s. 4d. to Hocking for the week & he gone home by the Gilliver boat, his wife poorly he says. Roster now 17. Lamp oil two gallons remaining, the boat to bring more Sat. if it come. [Transcriber's note: the original is very faded below this line.]

units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Dec. 5th. Felled 38. A rule made at supper by Mr Trevail that no man go beyond the lamps after the light fails, & that the lamps be kept in all night at the cook-house & the bunk-house both. Some grumbling at the oil. I have wrote the rule in this book as he bid me. 'Watch ye therefore.' Roster 17.

units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Dec. 8th. Gale from the S.W., no work. Rowe & young Pascoe asked for their wages to go home, & Mr Trevail would not pay before the month end. Hard words at the cook-house door. Pascoe said he would swim it. He did not. Roster 17 but two not working. Tally for the week 162.

units.title: 'Our Gilliver Correspondent', autumn 1911: the quarantine story
units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: Editor's note. The column below appeared in the issue of 14 October 1911, page 6. It is the earliest appearance in our pages of the story that the Holm once held a quarantine station. The paper printed a correction from the same correspondent a week later, which we shall reproduce in turn. We give both because the rumour has outlived the correction by more than a century.

units.author: courier_1890s
units.text: We hear, though we do not vouch for it, that the old station upon the Holm was in former years a place of quarantine for ships' crews brought in sick from the northern trade, and that the curing-house stands upon the foundations of a lazaretto. Your correspondent has this from a gentleman lately come from Port Ammet, who had it from his grandmother, and we set it down as it was told to us.

units.title: Kittering Holm fish-curing station (wiki)
units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: The fish-curing station on Kittering Holm operated from c.1880 to 1931, salting and barrelling herring and, later, ling for the northern trade. Structures recorded: two salting sheds, a cooperage, a stone jetty and a foreman's cottage. Seasonal staff of around thirty, mostly Gilliver women employed as gutters, crossed daily by boat. It closed after the herring collapse. The persistent 'quarantine station' story has no support in harbour, parish or Lights Board records.[1]

units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: Talk. The Lisle School project of 1991, 'The Holm in Our Grandparents' Time', has been added to the Society's holdings by kind permission of Mrs Hale (ref. MSHS/ED/1991/4). It records three grandparents' recollections of the 1890s timber camp: two give wages as the reason for its abandonment, one gives 'the dark'. Editors are asked not to promote either reading into the main article. [Citation needed: who first said 'the dark'?]

units.title: Talk: Holm timber camp (1894-95), reason for abandonment
units.author: hist_wiki_pell
units.text: This claim is poorly sourced. The article says the camp was 'abandoned in midwinter in unexplained circumstances'. The Penhallow diary records the foreman refusing to pay wages before the month end and men asking to leave (8 Dec.). A pay dispute in a hard winter explains an abandonment perfectly well and needs nothing 'unexplained'. Proposed wording: 'abandoned in midwinter following a dispute over wages'.

units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: The diary also records the lamp rule on 5 Dec., three days before any dispute. I'd resist 'following' as a statement of cause; 'during' is all the source supports. Suggested compromise: 'abandoned in midwinter; the clerk's diary records a dispute over wages in its final weeks'. That keeps the record and leaves the reader to weigh it.

units.title: Miss Arnell's Holm notebook, 1923 (third and fourth days)
units.author: naturalist_1923
units.text: Third day on the Holm. Excellent browse throughout: bramble and holly cropped by nothing, ivy reaching the ground on the oaks, rowan seedlings untouched in every clearing. No slots, no droppings, no rubbed bark, no lying-up places. I have walked the ridge twice. Either Cervus insularis has never swum the nine kilometres, or I am a poor naturalist. My boatman favours the second.

units.author: naturalist_1923
units.text: Fourth day. Wind W., fair. Song thrush, wren, three goldcrests in the spruce [sketch of a goldcrest, unfinished]. A heron working the curing-station jetty; the sheds are empty now but the smell of salt herring remains in the boards. Hollin, my boatman, again would not stay ashore after four o'clock. He says it is his supper. I said I had sandwiches. He was not moved.

units.title: Catalogue LBA-0214 and LBA-0215 (Brackwater, 1980s)
units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: LBA-0214. Date: winter 1984, day not recorded. Location: Brackwater reservoir, north shore. Kit: portable cassette recorder, built-in microphone. Duration: 22 min 40 s. Content: wind, distant traffic, a dog. Three percussive events at 11:02 to 11:09 on the tape counter, unattributed. Recordist's note on the card: 'gate?' Curator's note: there was no gate on that stretch of shore in 1984.

units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: LBA-0215. Date: 1986. Location: Brackwater Woods, pumping house track. Kit: open-reel portable, dynamic microphone. Duration: 31 min. Content: rain, the pumping house motor (a steady hum with harmonics), tawny owls. No percussive events. Provenance: donated with LBA-0214 by the same family. Curator's note: included for completeness. Not every Brackwater tape knocks.

units.title: Rendle diary, winter 1934
units.author: fisher_diary_1930s
units.text: Nov 30. Wind SW stiff. Hauled the Holm pots, 40, lobster 6 small 1 good, brown crab poor. Price at Ammet 1s 9d. The curing house roof is going, slates off the west side, nobody to mend it now. Mother lit the lamp at four. Brother Jory says he wont go Holm side again till spring and wont say why. He is a fool and I told him so.

units.title: The great gale of 1953, from the back issues
units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: Editor's note. With a storm forecast for the Sound this week, several readers have asked what the last 'great gale' looked like in these pages. Tomorrow we reproduce the front page of 2 February 1953 in full. A warning in advance: the headline writer's spelling of Tollinby is his own, and he was not corrected for three issues.
